  2. Driving southwest through flat desert. Driving direction is different than on E38 for most of the section.
  3. Driving north through green plains with very cloudy weather.
  4. R-278 is a divided highway, unlike the other roads. M-36 is driven northeast through green plains under sunny conditions. At Fyodorovka, the car turns north.

Note: The same clean car can also appear on various other roads near major cities, so use this clue with caution.

lm.name: Clean Car with a Wire and a Bracket in the Green Plains
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Clean Car with a Wire and a Bracket (image 2):

  1. M-36, starting at Fyodorovka and driving northwest up to the Russian border.
  2. A-21, starting at Ukatkan and driving northeast up to the intersection near Pokrovka.

The car on these roads has no visible dots, smudges, or other marks. The coverage was captured in summer, and the landscape is flat and green.

You can distinguish these sections by driving direction and car meta.

  1. Driving northwest — if you see a long line of trucks, you're very close to the border with Russia.
  2. Driving northeast — west of Presnovka, the car has a dot between the metal holders (image 3), which is not present further east.

Note: The same clean car can also appear on various other roads near major cities, so use this clue with caution.

lm.name: Clean Car without a Wire
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Clean Car without a Wire (image 2):

  1. R-211, starting at the intersection near Akkol, driving east to the intersection with R-212 and continuing north up to Stepnogorsk.
  2. A17, starting at the intersection with P4 and driving south up to the suburbs of Karaganda.
  3. R-190, starting at Sarana, driving southwest to Shakhtinsk, and from there east via R-187 up to the intersection with A17.

The car on these roads has no visible dots, smudges, or other marks. The coverage was done in autumn.

You can distinguish these two roads by driving direction, weather and car meta:

  1. Driving east or northeast through green plains with tree clasters.
  2. Driving south or southwest through rolling, grassy hills.
  3. Driving through grassy fields with sparse trees. Buildings are often visible in the distance.

Note: The same clean can appear on other roads near larger cities, so use this clue with caution.

lm.name: Clean Car without a Wire on the Divided Highway in Autumn
lm.note:
The following divided highways (image 1) are covered by this Clean Car without a Wire (image 2):

  1. A17, starting at the intersection northwest of the Сасық көл lake and driving west up to the intersection with P4.
  2. P4, starting at the intersection near Turgay and driving southwest up to Astana.
  3. M-36, starting in the suburbs of Astana driving southeast up to the intersection near Osakarovka.
  4. M-36, starting south of Temirtau, driving north around the city up to Pokornoe.

These are the most commonly appearing divided highways, which were covered by the Clean Car without a Wire. You can distinguish these roads by driving direction and the weather.

  1. Driving west in sunny weather.
  2. Driving west or southwest with puffy clouds scattered across the sky. The car is blurred for a short stretch near Turgay, but the cloudy autumn coverage is still very recognizable.
  3. Driving southeast under a completely clear sky.
  4. Driving northwest or northeast in very sunny conditions.

Note: The same clean car can appear on other divided highways near larger cities, so use this clue with caution.

lm.name: Dirty Car on the Divided Highway
lm.note:
The following divided highway (image 1) is covered by this Dirty Car (image 2):

– A1, starting in the suburbs of Kokshetau and driving southeast around Shchuchinsk up to the intersection with R-228.

lm.name: Dirty Car with 1 Dot on the Right
lm.note:

  • A3, starting from the intersection above Konaev (Avtomobil'nyy Most), driving northeast, passing around Saryozek and continuing via A353 east to the intersection near Kakinino, then turning south and ending near Нұрым, close to Altyn Emel National Park.

Bonus: If you see this car driving through the city and there are poles painted yellow and red (image 3), you must be in Saryozek.

lm.name: Dirty Car with 2 Lines on the Back – Non-Urban
lm.note:
The following road (image 1) is covered by this Dirty Car with 2 Lines on the Back (image 2):

  • A353, starting at the intersection near Kalinino and driving east up to the border with China.

Note 1: Sometimes the car has two dots in the middle visible in the image, sometimes just one, and occasionally none are visible.

lm.name: Dirty Car with 2 Lines on the Back – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and you see this Dirty Car with 2 Lines on the Back (image 1), you are most likely in the northern part of Almaty.

Note 1: Sometimes the car has two dots in the middle visible in the image, sometimes just one, and occasionally none are visible.

Note 2: This car also covered the A353, which occasionally passes through towns and villages such as Zharkenet, Malaya, Bol’shoy Shygan, and Пенжім. Since the A353 is a major highway, if you're on a busy road with a lot of vehicles and the car is driving east, consider these locations as well.

lm.name: Dirty Car with a Lot of Dots
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Dirty Car with a Lot of Dots (image 2):

  1. R-217, starting at Atbasar suburbs, driving southeast to the intersection with R-260, and continuing up to the intersection with A-16.
  2. R-217 off-road, starting at the intersection east of Kiyma, driving south and then west to Trudovoye.

The weather on these roads is generally cloudy. The sun is visible only near the suburbs of Atbasar and on the off-road section of R-217.

You can distinguish these sections by the presence of pavement and the landscape:

  1. R-217 main road and R-260 are both paved:
    • R-217 is very flat.
    • R-260 is more hilly, and in the final few kilometers, the pavement quality becomes very poor and eventually disappears entirely.
  2. R-217 off-road is unpaved, but remains very flat, unlike the more uneven terrain of R-260.

Note 1: If you're in a semi-urban area and see this car, you're most likely in the suburbs of Derzhavinsk.

Note 2: A similar dirty car covers R-214 between Kokshetau and Atbasar, but that car has a bracket — unlike the one used on the roads south of Atbasar.

lm.name: East Kazakhstan/Abai Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the East Kazakhstan Region is 16. Abai Region officially uses 18, but it was formed in June 2022 by separating from the East Kazakhstan Region, so in practice, the vast majority of vehicles there still carry the East Kazakhstan Region code.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Eastern Karaganda Car with 3 Dots on the Left – Urban
lm.note: If you are in an urban area and see this Car with 3 Dots on the Left (image 1), you must be in the eastern part of Karaganda (image 2).

lm.name: Ekibastuz Pole Paint
lm.note:
In Ekibastuz, poles are commonly painted white with a short light blue stripe at the top (image 1).

Be careful — this paint scheme is also used in Ereymentau and Doskey, but you can differentiate the cities by their street layouts: Ereymentau follows a north-south grid, Doskey northwest-southeast, and Ekibastuz northeast-southwest.

Note: Additionally, poles with the same color scheme are occasionally found in a few villages in southern Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Ereymentau Car with 1 Dot on the Right – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and see this Car with 1 Dot on the Right (image 1), you must be in Ereymentau or its suburbs.

Note: It is hard to spot this dot, but it is very useful as it only appears in this village.

lm.name: Ereymentau Pole Paint
lm.note:
In Ereymentau, poles are sometimes painted white with a short light blue stripe at the top (image 1).

Be careful — this paint scheme is also used in Ekibastuz and Doskey, but you can differentiate the cities by their street layout. Ereymentau follows a north-south grid, Doskey northwest-southeast, and Ekibastuz northeast-southwest.

Note 1: This paint scheme is used for poles holding street lamps. Poles without mounted lamps are likely either unpainted or use the Akmola color scheme.

Note 2: Additionally, poles with the same color scheme are occasionally found in a few villages in southern Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Forest Fire Coverage
lm.note:
In the southern part of Oskemen (image 1) the coverage was done during a forest fire at sunset, giving the sky an orange/pink hue and making it very cloudy (image 2).

You can occasionally see black smoke.

lm.name: Fort-Shevchenko Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note: Street signs in Fort-Shevchenko have white text on a blue background, enclosed in a black metal frame with a pointed end (image 1).

lm.name: Gas Boxes
lm.note:
In front of the houses in Taldykorgan, Taraz, Shymkent, Turkistan, and Kentau, you’ll often spot gas boxes connected to external gas pipes. The boxes are usually yellow, though occasionally they may be grey (image 1).

How to differentiate these cities:

  • Taldykorgan has late winter coverage. You can often see snow lying around.
  • Taraz was covered in early spring, so you’ll notice trees just beginning to grow leaves. In most cases, the gas boxes here are grey, unlike in other cities.
  • Shymkent was covered in late spring, which makes the grass appear super-green — a generally good clue for this city. Occasionally, the gas boxes here will also be grey instead of yellow.
  • Turkistan has summer coverage, and the grass appears drier than in Shymkent.
  • Kentau looks similar to Turkistan, but it’s covered by a clean car without a bracket. In contrast, Turkistan is typically covered by either a car with a bracket, a car with 4 stripes and a dirty roof, or a car with numerous grey dots on the roof.

Be careful — gas boxes may also appear occasionally in other cities.

lm.name: Jambyl Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Jambyl Region is 08.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Karaganda Bus Stops
lm.note:
In Karaganda, you can commonly see turquoise bus stops with curved roofs and yellow benches (image 1). They typically have two yellow trash bins — one on each side of the shelter.

Note 1: Occasionally, you might spot a bus stop with a slightly different design, but the color scheme remains the same (image 2).

Note 2: The same turquoise color is also used for city buses.

lm.name: Karaganda Buses
lm.note:
In Karaganda, you can commonly see these turquoise buses (image 1).

Note 1: The same turquoise color is also used for bus stops in the city.

Note 2: I’ve seen a bus with the same color once or twice in Uralsk.

lm.name: Karaganda/Ulytau Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Karaganda Region is 09. Ulytau Region officially uses 20, but it was formed in June 2022 by separating from Karaganda Region, so in practice, the vast majority of vehicles there still carry the Karaganda Region code.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Kentau Pole Paint
lm.note: Kentau consistently uses a pole paint scheme consisting of a short blue stripe, followed by yellow and red stripes, then a longer section of blue, with the bottom of the pole painted black (image 1).

lm.name: Kokshetau Buses
lm.note:
There are two types of buses commonly seen in Kokshetau. Both share the same color scheme: they are white with orange mirrors and an orange lower part (image 1).

On the sides, one model has the white 'INVIVO' text on a red background, while the other features "OLYMP" written on a white background, along with an orange roof.

Note: Similar buses can occasionally be spotted in Shymkent, but they feature the Shymkent city logo on the side (image 2).

lm.name: Kokshetau Pole Paint
lm.note:
Kokshetau occasionally uses a pole paint scheme consisting of a short yellow stripe, followed by a longer section of light blue, then another short yellow stripe, with the rest of the pole painted light blue down to the bottom (image 1).

Some poles feature a yellow graphic between the two stripes. Occasionally, the yellow parts are missing, there’s only one stripe, or the stripe color differs from yellow.

Overall, this paint scheme is quite inconsistent.

lm.name: Kokshetau Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
Street signs in Kokshetau have black text in either Cyrillic or Latin on white background, enclosed in a white metal frame with one rounded side (image 1).

Be careful, as very similar signs can be found in many different cities but with a black frame instead of white (image 2). Also, don't confuse them with Taldykorgan signs, which have a frame rounded from both sides and are always attached to the traffic light poles (image 3).

Note: I once saw a similar sign in a random town in the south of the country.

lm.name: Konaev Cars – Urban
lm.note:
In Konaev and the surrounding roads (excluding the A3 highway) you will encounter only one of these two cars (image 1):

  1. A type car with 4 stripes and a dirty back.
  2. B type car with a bracket and the boomerang-shaped smudge on the left.

No other car types, apart from these two, are found in this area. The map indicates where you can find them (image 1). On the A3 highway you can spot Konaev A type car only in the small section marked on the map.

Sometimes the car in the city is blurred, but if you believe you are in this region, you can still use the car antenna to distinguish between the northern and southern parts.

  1. A type car has a folded antenna.
  2. B type car has an antenna with 8 stripes.

Be careful. In urban areas, the same A type car, with a slightly dirtier roof, can be found in north-western suburbs of Almaty and eastern Kaskelen. However, the coverage in those areas was likely done later, causing the car to have additional smudges (image 2).

The coverage in Almaty/Kaskelen was done during the sunset, with a really cloudy sky, while in Konaev the sun is high, and there isn't a single cloud in the sky.

lm.name: Koschi Vibes – Urban
lm.note:
The coverage in Koschi, a small city in Akmola south of Astana, was taken in November during a period of heavy overcast. The vegetation appears lifeless, while the soil has a distinct orange hue.

The area is undergoing extensive development, with many roads freshly paved and the sidewalks either newly laid or still under construction. Dark gravel is scattered throughout, and the asphalt is intensely black. Most of the buildings in the city are made from yellow and orange brick.

The overall scenery is shown in image 1.

lm.name: Kostanay Bus Stops
lm.note: In Kostanay, you can occasionally spot these simple brown bus stops featuring the city's logo on the glass (image 1).

lm.name: Kostanay Pole Paint
lm.note: In Kostanay, poles are commonly painted yellow with a short green stripe at the top (image 1).

lm.name: Kostanay Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Kostanay Region is 10.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Kostanay Region Pedestrian Traffic Lights
lm.note:
On major intersections in Kostanay and Rudny, you can find pedestrian traffic lights with countdown timers and black text on a yellow background (image 1).

In Rudny, the text is more often written in the Latin alphabet, while in Kostanay it's typically in Cyrillic — though this isn't a strict rule, and sometimes there is no text at all.

It’s almost impossible to get a location in Rudny with these signs without also seeing the distinctive Rudny pole paint. So, if you spot one of these signs without any painted poles nearby, you’re most likely in Kostanay.

lm.name: Kulsary Street Lamps
lm.note:
In Kulsary, you can find these street lamps with exceptionally tall photocell mounted on top (image 1).

Note: Photocells are also present in other cities, but they are usually much smaller and barely noticeable.

lm.name: Kulsary Surface-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
In Kulsary you can find these street signs attached to fences or buildings with house number, where half of the space is occupied by a QR code (image 1).

Be careful — similar signs can be found in Aktobe, but there the house number is inside a circle (image 2).

lm.name: Kyzylorda Lamp Post Paint
lm.note: In Kyzylorda, lamp posts are commonly painted turquoise with two thin white stripes at the top (image 1).

lm.name: Kyzylorda Pole Paint
lm.note: In Kyzylorda, poles are commonly painted with two stripes — red and yellow — followed by white (occasionally turquoise) extending to the bottom (image 1).

lm.name: Kyzylorda Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Kyzylorda Region is 11.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Mangystau Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Mangystau Region is 12.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: May Coverage
lm.note:
Alataou (image 1), a small settlement 25 km east of Almaty, is the only place in Kazakhstan that was covered in May. Snow-capped mountains are visible to the south, the weather is very sunny, and the vegetation is lush green (image 2) — unlike in the surrounding areas, which were covered in winter.

Note: You can confirm this clue by checking for the presence of the wire in the car trunk (image 3).

lm.name: Nearly Clean Car with a Wire and a Bracket in the Desert
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Nearly Clean Car with a Wire and a Bracket (image 2):

  1. An unlabeled road starting from Aktau, driving northwest, bypassing Aqshuqyr, passing through Aktau Airport, and continuing up to Fort-Schevchenko.
  2. An unlabeled road starting from Zhanaozen and driving south to the Turkmenistan border.
  3. An unlabeled road starting from Zhanaozen and driving generally in the northeast direction to Beket-Ata.

The car on these roads might be slightly dirty, but it lacks the characteristic dots, smudges, or other marks. The surrounding landscape is desert, and the weather is sunny, with the sun high in the sky.

You can distinguish these three sections by driving direction.

Note 1: Cars with a wire and a bracket on other roads may also appear nearly clean because dirt patterns are hard to see under intense sunlight.

Note 2: A similar car can also appear on various other roads near major cities, so use this clue with caution.

lm.name: Nearly Clean Car with a Wire and a Bracket on the Divided Highway in the Desert
lm.note:
The following road (image 1) is covered by this Nearly Clean Car with a Wire and a Bracket (image 2):

  • A-33, starting at the roundabout south of Mangystau, driving east, then continuing on R-114 and proceeding east up to the intersection west of Zhanaozen.

The car is slightly dirty, but it lacks the characteristic dots, smudges, or other marks. The surrounding landscape is desert, and the weather is sunny with sparse clouds in the sky. The coverage was captured at sunrise, and the farther east you go, the higher the sun appears in the sky.

Note: The same clean car can appear on other divided highways near larger cities, so use this clue with caution.

lm.name: North Kazakhstan Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the North Kazakhstan Region is 15.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Oskemen Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, a 'Leaf' Smudge, and 1 Line of Dirt – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and see this Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, a 'Leaf' Smudge, and 1 Line of Dirt (image 1), you must be in the northern suburbs of Oskemen.

Note 1: A car with the same 'leaf' smudge but without any noticeable dirt lines on the roof also appears in Semey. There is also a second variant of this car in Oskemen, which features 2 lines of dirt instead of 1. Note 2: There are also many different cars with one or more leaves on the roof, so be cautious.

lm.name: Oskemen Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, a 'Leaf' Smudge, and 2 Lines of Dirt – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and see this Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, a 'Leaf' Smudge, and 2 Lines of Dirt (image 1), you must be in Oskemen.

Note 1: A car with the same 'leaf' smudge but without any noticeable dirt lines on the roof also appears in Semey. There is also a second variant of this car in Oskemen, which features 1 line of dirt instead of 2. Note 2: There are also many different cars with one or more leaves on the roof, so be cautious.

lm.name: Partly Blurred 3-Part Car in the Desert
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Partly Blurred 3-Part Car (image 2):

  1. R-114/A-33, starting halfway between the intersection with E-121 and the road curve, driving west up to Aktau.
  2. A-33, starting on the intersection with R-114, driving roughly north up to Aisha Bibi cafe hotel near Say-Otes.

You can distinguish these roads by driving direction, amount of roadways, and car meta:

  1. Driving west on a divided highway. The car has three dots on the roof, although sometimes not all of them are visible (image 3).
  2. Driving north, east, or northeast on a single roadway and the car has no dots on the roof.

Note 1: The same car can also be found in the northern, greener parts of Kazakhstan, as well as in urban areas and the suburbs of larger cities.

Note 2: On the A-33 section close to Aktau, you may also spot a Car with Orange Dirt in the Bottom Left.

lm.name: Partly Blurred 3-Part Car in the Green Plains
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Partly Blurred 3-Part Car (image 2):

  1. A1, starting in Petropavl, driving south up to the roundabout near Kellerovka.
  2. R-247, starting at the intersection with A1 near Makinsk, driving northeast to the center of Stepnyak.

You can distinguish these roads by driving direction and weather:

  1. Sunny coverage and driving south. From Petropavl to the intersection with A-16, the road is a 3-way divided highway.
  2. Cloudy coverage and driving northeast.

Note: The same car can also be found in the southwestern, desert regions of Kazakhstan, as well as in urban areas and the suburbs of larger cities.

lm.name: Pavlodar Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks. The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Pavlodar Region is 14.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Pedestrian Signs Attached Sideways
lm.note:
The vast majority of pedestrian signs in Karaganda and nearby cities are mounted sideways (image 1) to traffic light poles, rather than on separate vertical rods (it applies only to pedestrian crossings controlled by traffic lights). These signs usually lack the yellow reflective border commonly seen elsewhere.

Be careful — sideways-mounted pedestrian signs can be found in other cities as well, just less frequently. However, if you see multiple signs without yellow outlines mounted this way, you're likely in the Karaganda region.

Bonus tip: In Astana, pedestrian signs are never used at crossings controlled by traffic lights. It can help in 50:50 cases between Karaganda and Astana.

lm.name: Petropavl Bus Stops
lm.note:
In Petropavl, you can commonly see brown bus stops with a roof angled slightly upwards and a bench mounted asymmetrically on the right side (image 1).

Note: Similar bus stops can be found in Stepnogorsk, but there the bench is mounted symmetrically, unlike in Petropavl.

lm.name: Petropavl Buses
lm.note:
In Petropavl, you can commonly see these white buses with a green pattern on the side (image 1).

Be careful not to confuse them with Astana buses, which look very similar but also include black in their color scheme.

If you're unsure which one of these buses you see, check whether the car has a wire in the top left part of the truck bed. In Petropavl, the wire is present — in Astana, it's not (image 2).

Note: the wire may look slightly different or might not be visible due to the car blur.

lm.name: Petropavl car with 4 Stripes, a Smudge, and a Dot on the Right – Urban
lm.note:
If you see this Car with 4 Stripes, a Smudge, and a Dot on the Right (image 1), you must be in southeastern Petropavl or on the roads east of the city.

Note: The smudge is sometimes hardly visible.

lm.name: Petropavl Pole Paint
lm.note: In Petropavl, poles are commonly painted grey with a short white stripe at the top (image 1).

lm.name: Petropavl Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note: Pole-mounted street signs in Petropavl have white text in both Kazakh and Russian, divided by an arrow, on a green background, enclosed in a white metal frame with a pointed end (image 1).

lm.name: Petropavl Surface-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note: In Petropavl, you can commonly find these white and blue street signs attached to fences or buildings, where the house number is placed inside a blue semi-ellipse that is joined to the bottom of the rectangular nameplate (image 1).

lm.name: Poor Quality Roads
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are in very poor condition (image 2):

  1. A-26, starting from the intersection with E38 and driving southwest to Shalkar.
  2. A-26, starting from Shalkar and driving northwest to a point roughly halfway between Izembet and Dzhurun.

Both roads are either unpaved or have badly damaged pavement. The surrounding landscape is desert-like, and the coverage was captured under overcast skies.

You can distinguish these roads by driving direction and car meta:

  1. Driving southwest. Coverage was done by a car with 4 stripes and a white sticker.
  2. Driving Northwest. The road was covered by three different cars:
  • From Shalkar to Berchogur: A car without a bracket (a short stretch near Shalkar features a blurred car).
  • From Berchogur to Talysay: A car with a bracket and a visible scratch.
  • North of Talysay: A car with a bracket but no scratch.

Note: The car may appear blurred in some places.

lm.name: Ridder Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, and a Leaf – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and see this Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, and a Leaf (image 1), you must be in Ridder.

The coverage in Ridder is quite distinctive anyway — with high mountains surrounding the city and consistently overcast weather — but this car can still help confirm your location.

Note: There are many different cars with one or more leaves on the roof, so be cautious.

lm.name: Road Through Rolling Hills and Grassy Fields
lm.note: There is no meta for the road between Shymkent and Zhetisay (image 1), but it has a unique vibe. The car drives south through rolling, grassy hills (image 2). It's very sunny, without a single cloud in the sky. The A-2 section is a divided highway. After leaving the A-2, the road becomes a single roadway.

lm.name: Roads in the Snowy Mountains
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are the highly recognizable as they pass through high mountain terrain:

  1. Unlabeled road from Almaty to the Big Almaty Lake.
  2. Unlabeled road from Almaty to Shymbulak ski resort.

You can distinguish these two sections by the amount of snow and car meta.

  1. This road is covered by a very dirty car (top of image 2), and some stretches of the road are covered with snow.
  2. This road is covered by a less dirty car with a bracket (bottom of image 2) or a clean car with a scratch, and the snow is melting or mostly gone.

Note 1: There is another mountain road in the area that is covered by a different car — be careful not to mix them up.

Note 2: The very dirty car (top of image 2) also appears in Almaty and Kaskelen.

lm.name: Rudny Pole Paint
lm.note:
Rudny commonly uses a pole paint scheme consisting of a short red stripe, followed by yellow, then another red stripe, with the rest of the pole painted white down to the bottom (image 1).

Note: The color arrangement somewhat resembles the Spanish flag.

lm.name: Semey Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, a 'Leaf' Smudge, and a Dirty Back – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and see this Car with 4 Stripes, a Tilted Antenna, a 'Leaf' Smudge, and a Dirty Back (image 1), you must be in Semey.

Occasionally, the leaf that caused the smudge is still attached to the roof of the car (image 2).

Note 1: A car with the same 'leaf' smudge but with noticeable dirt lines on the roof, also appears in Oskemen.

Note 2: There are also many different cars with one or more leaves on the roof, so be cautious.

lm.name: Semey Car with Black Dirt on the Roof – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and you see this Car with Black Dirt on the Roof (image 1), you must be in the northern suburbs of Semey.

Note: Occasionally, you may spot leaves lying on the roof.

lm.name: Shchuchinsk Pole Paint
lm.note:
In Shchuchinsk, poles are rarely painted yellow with a short red stripe at the top (image 1).

Be careful — similar pole markings can also be found in Atbasar, Derzhavinsk, Kandyagash, and Tobyl. Here are some tips to help tell them apart:

  • In Atbasar, the yellow paint appears more like a cream color, as if yellow and white were mixed.
  • In Derzhavinsk, the coverage was done during overcast weather by the dirty car with a lot of dots (top part of image 2).
  • In Kandyagash, the coverage was done by the car with a bracket and dirty back (medium part of image 2).
  • In Tobyl, the coverage was done by the car with 4 stripes and a white sticker (bottom part of image 2).

lm.name: Shymkent Bus
lm.note:
In Shymkent, you can commonly spot these eco-friendly, gas-powered Yutong buses painted in a light green and white color scheme (image 1).

These buses are also used in other cities across Kazakhstan, but if you can see the side of the bus, you can distinguish it by the presence of the red Shymkent logo. Its color stands out against the background, even from a distance.

Note: Sometimes the bus may be dirty, making the logo less visible.

lm.name: Shymkent License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks. The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for Shymkent is 17. Shymkent was separated from South Kazakhstan Region (which was simultaneously renamed Turkistan Region) in June 2018, so this area code is still relatively rare, as many vehicles there still have the 13 region code.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Shymkent Pole Paint
lm.note:
In Shymkent, poles are rarely painted with two stripes — red and yellow — followed by dark green down to the bottom (image 1). The red paint is sometimes faded and difficult to see.

Be careful — similarly painted poles can be found in cities south of Shymkent, but they include an additional red stripe beneath the yellow.

lm.name: Shymkent Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
Street signs in Shymkent have white text with Kazakh, Russian, and English words for 'street' on a blue background (image 1). They are attached to a metal frame, which is usually rusted.

Be careful — similar signs can be found in Zhetisay, but the metal frame has a pointed end and the word 'street' is written only in Kazakh (image 2).

Note: The same street signs appear in the cities, along the road from Shymkent to Zhetisay.

lm.name: Stepnogorsk Bus Stops
lm.note:
In Stepnogorsk, you can commonly see these brown bus stops with a roof angled slightly upwards and a bench mounted on the bottom of the horizontal bar (image 1). They typically feature two brown trash bins, one on each side of the bus stop.

Note: Similar bus stops can be found in Petropavl, but there the bench is mounted asymmetrically, unlike in Stepnogorsk.

lm.name: Stepnogorsk Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
Street signs in Stepnogorsk have black text on a white background, enclosed in a black metal frame with a pointed end (image 1).

Be careful — very similar signs can be found in many other cities, but with a metal frame that is rounded at the end instead of pointed (image 2).

Note: From a distance, the frame may sometimes appear rounded because the inner surface of the sign has a semi-circular end, even if the actual metal frame is pointed.

lm.name: Taldykorgan Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
Street signs in Taldykorgan have black text on a white background, enclosed in a white metal frame rounded on both sides (image 1). They are attached on their backs to traffic light poles.

Be careful — similar signs can be found in Kokshetau, but they are side-attached to a metal pole designed exclusively for them, and the frame is rounded only on one side (image 2).

lm.name: Taraz Pole Paint
lm.note:
Taraz consistently uses a pole paint scheme consisting of a short red stripe, followed by a longer yellow section, with the bottom of the pole painted black (image 1).

Note: In Shakbak Baba, the lamp posts are painted similarly to poles in Taraz, with red, yellow, and black stripes — but you can distinguish that location by the presence of large hills to the south.

lm.name: Trams
lm.note:
Trams (image 1) can be found in Pavlodar, Oskemen, and Temirtau.

You can distinguish these cities by tram appearance, line orientation and car meta:

  • Trams in Pavlodar are more modern than those in Oskemen and Temirtau. They often feature a red-and-white design. Sometimes they use other colors, but they are usually covered with advertisements and generally look clean and well-maintained.

  • Trams in Temirtau and Oskemen have older designs and look quite similar. They typically have a blue (sometimes red) and white color scheme, and may also be covered in graffiti. You can tell these two cities apart using other clues:

    All of Temirtau was covered by a clean car. In Oskemen, several car types were used, but the sections near the tram lines were covered either by a dirty car or by a car with a bracket.

    You can also use the street orientation as a clue — I’ve marked all tram lines in both cities on the map (image 2).

Note 1: You can also find the remnants of tram infrastructure in Almaty, so if you see only tram tracks, consider that city as well.

Note 2: Be careful not to confuse tram tracks with train tracks, which are visible in various cities.

lm.name: Turkistan Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the Turkistan Region is 13.

It is worth knowing that Shymkent, which uses the 17 region code, was separated from South Kazakhstan Region (which was simultaneously renamed Turkistan Region) in June 2018, so many vehicles there still have the 13 area code.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: Turkistan Street Lamps
lm.note:
In Turkistan you can find these thin grey street lamps with two (sometimes three) light sources and two rectangular grey stripes (image 1).

Be careful — similar-looking lamps can be found in other cities as well.

Note: I’ve seen these lamps on one street in Almaty and on one street in Astana.

lm.name: Uralsk Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
These distinct street signs with blue text on a white background and simple or ornamental arrows can only be found in Uralsk on Dostyk Druzhby Avenue (image 1).

They are found exclusively at the intersections marked on the map.

lm.name: Uralsk Street Lamps
lm.note: In Uralsk, you can find these street lamps with three separate lights arranged in an ascending pattern (image 1).

lm.name: Very Dirty Car – Non-Urban
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Very Dirty Car (image 2):

  • A3, starting in the suburbs of Almaty, driving north, turning northeast at the intersection near Ravlekatel'nyy Tsentr Dos, then continuing west via unlabeled road to A351, turning slightly southeast and finishing at the off-road path leading to Charyn Canyon National Park.

On the divided highway, the car drives in both directions. In Almaty, it started the trip at dawn, so the further east you go, the sunnier it gets. On the return journey (driving west), the sun is low, but it gets progressively lower the closer you get to Almaty.

On the divided section of the highway heading west, the car is blurred between Baydibek Biy and Koyshibek, but you can still recognize the road thanks to the sunset coverage and the white mountains visible to the south.

Note: There are several dirty cars in Kazakhstan, but the smudge patterns vary, so be careful not to confuse them.

lm.name: Very Dirty Car – Urban
lm.note:
If you are in an urban area and you see this Very Dirty Car (top part of image 1), you have to be in the northwestern suburbs of Almaty or eastern Kaskelen (image 2).

Be careful — the same car, with a slightly less dirty roof, can also be found in urban areas around Konaev, but it was likely covered earlier, so it has fewer smudges (bottom part of image 1).

Coverage in Almaty and Kaskelen is captured during sunset under a very cloudy sky, while in Konaev, the sun is high and the sky is completely clear.

lm.name: Very Dirty Car with 2 Dots
lm.note:
The following roads (image 1) are covered by this Very Dirty Car with 2 Dots (image 2):

  • A-351, starting at the intersection near the Charyn Canyon Monument Sign, driving south, then turning onto P-16 and continuing west up to Kolsay Lakes.

The first section of the route is relatively flat, with low hills surrounding the area. As you approach Kolsay Lakes, the terrain becomes increasingly mountainous.

Note: There are several dirty cars in Kazakhstan, but their smudge patterns vary, so pay close attention to avoid confusion.

lm.name: Very Dirty Car with a Bracket
lm.note:
The following road (image 1) is covered by this Very Dirty Car with a Bracket (image 2):

  • R-214, starting at Kokshetau and driving south to Atbasar.

From Kokshetau to Zerenda, the car has noticeable 'vertical smudges' on the roof (top part of image 2). Around Zerenda, it begins to rain and the road becomes wet — the smudges get washed off, but the car remains very dirty (bottom part of image 2). As you approach Atbasar, the sun begins to set. The coverage on this road was done in autumn during overcast weather.

Note: A similar dirty car covers R-217 and R-260 south of Atbasar, but that one lacks a bracket — unlike the car used on R-214.

lm.name: West Kazakhstan Region License Plate Code
lm.note:
In Kazakhstan, you can occasionally spot license plates on the rear of buses and trucks (image 1). The last two digits of a license plate indicate the region of registration.

The area code for the West Kazakhstan Region is 07.

Note: Since vehicles often travel between regions, use this clue cautiously. It’s more reliable when seen on local public transport or smaller commercial vehicles than on long-distance trucks.

lm.name: West Kazakhstan Region Pole Paint
lm.note:
In the West Kazakhstan Region, poles are painted with red, white, and black (image 1).

Due to limited coverage, you can only spot them on the E38 running through Zhimpity and in Uralsk and its suburbs.

lm.name: Zhanaozen Street Lamps
lm.note:
In Zhanaozen you can find these thin grey street lamps with four light sources that resemble a fly swatter (image 1).

Be careful — as similar-looking lamps can be found in other cities as well.

lm.name: Zhetisay Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
In Zhetisay, you can commonly find pole-mounted street signs with white text on a blue background, enclosed in a metal frame that is often rusted and has a pointed end (image 1).

Be careful — similar signs appear in Shymkent and in towns along the road from Shymkent to Zhetisay, but they lack the pointed end (image 2).

lm.name: Zhetisay Surface-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
In Zhetisay, you can commonly find blue street signs attached to fences or buildings. They feature a white inner line that doesn’t touch the edges of the sign, with a QR code on the right side (image 1).

While the design may seem fairly generic, these details make the signs stand out.

lm.name: Zhezqazghan Bus Stops
lm.note: In Zhezqazghan, you can commonly spot these unique, wide turquoise bus stops featuring an indoor waiting room (image 1).

lm.name: Zhezqazghan Buses
lm.note: In Zhezqazghan, you can occasionally spot these white and yellow buses with "Men ♥ Jezz" written on the side (image 1). A less common version uses orange instead of yellow and features the text "Men ♥ Zhez" (image 2).

lm.name: Zhezqazghan Pole-Mounted Street Signs
lm.note:
Street signs in Zhezqazghan have black text on a white background, enclosed in a black metal frame with one rounded side (image 1). They feature a black inner line that doesn’t touch the edges of the sign, leaving white space between it and the metal frame. The signs are attached sideways to traffic light poles.

Additionaly on the intersections featuring these signs you can often spot this distnct rubbish bins, (image 2 - the color may vary).

Be careful — very similar signs can be found in many other cities, but those lack the black inner line, and their metal frame is doubled with free space in between (image 3).

lm.name: Zhezqazghan Scraped Roads
lm.note:
Many roads in Zhezqazghan are in poor condition and are undergoing maintenance. The top layer of asphalt is often scraped off, revealing shallow ruts on the layer beneath (image 1). Pieces of old asphalt are frequently scattered around, and construction machinery is commonly seen throughout the city.

Zhezqazghan is built on a small hill in a rather desert-like region, so the terrain is often inclined, and the vegetation tends to look dry.

Note: This meta isn’t very reliable, but if no stronger clues are available, it can still help.

  • Most strikingly, most of the rural coverage in Kazakhstan is in a very empty, open and mostly flat landscape.

lm.note:
• Like Russia, Kazakhstan uses yellow and white stripes on their pedestrian crossings.
  • However, unlike Russia the stripes often have white dashes on either side.
  • Sometimes, you can find the dashes without the stripes.

lm.note: • A lot of Kazakh infrastructure, from pedestrian signs, poles, houses, to bollards, is very similar to what you see in Russia.

lm.note: Kazakhstan uses a variety of post-Soviet style bollards, as well as ones that resemble Turkish bollards. Notably, the bollards seemingly consisting of two thin bollards attached at a 90° angle are unique to Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Autumn Hills
lm.note: The East Kazakhstan Region is hilly and forested. It was covered in october, so you will see fall colours on the vegetation. The town of Ridder itself is flat, but surrounded by hazy mountains.

lm.name: Birch Forests
lm.note:
These lush birch forests next to green fields are common in northern Kazakhstan.

NOTE: This landscape often appears very similar to that found in and around Omsk Oblast in Russia.

lm.name: Desert Landscape
lm.note: Sandy and shrubby desert-like landscapes are common in southwestern Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Grassy Rolling Hills
lm.note: Grassy green rolling hills can be found in southern Kazakhstan. They are especially common just north of Bishkek

lm.name: Green Plains
lm.note: Vast grassy green plains are found in northwestern Kazakhstan. They are especially common in Akmola and Kostanay regions.

lm.name: Tall Mountains
lm.note: Tall mountains, which are often snow-capped, can be seen in southeastern Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Uzbek Border
lm.note:
The landscape in southern Kazakhstan near Uzbekistan is hilly and quite dry and shrubby, with a lot of orange looking grass. The landscape consists of dry but grassy rolling hills or dead flat agricultural land near Zhetisay.

NOTE: These red and white KM markers that look like Kyrgyz ones, are only found near Zhetisay.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note: • Unlike neighbouring countries, Kazakhstan primarily uses yellow and black chevrons, except on T Intersections, where you will find the more generic red and white chevrons.

lm.note:
The only 6-lined divided highway in Kazakhstan.

It has yellow outer lines.

September coverage.

Mostly the sky is forecast, but the sun is still visible.

Quite a lot of trees along the higway .

lm.name: A1 Kokshetau-Petropavl
lm.note:
The only divided part of this road is near Petropavl.

Unblurred sides of the car.

White lines.

Summer coverage - sunny weather.

The further south you go, the less trees you can see.

The landscape is very flat and quite green.

lm.name: A2 Taraz-Almaty
lm.note:
This road is quite diverse.

The most part of the road is divided, with white lines.

However, yellow outer lines can also be seen.

Near Taraz, you will see mountains to the south.

The weather is mostly sunny, just near Almaty the sky is quite forecast.

The landscape is mostly flat, but some smaller hills can be seen in the distance.

March coverage - the vegetation is not lush or blooming.

lm.name: A2 Taraz-Shymkent
lm.note:
Divided highway with white lines (only near Taraz the road is not divided).

You will see snowy mountains to the south most of the times.

March coverage - weather is sunny with some clouds.

The landscape gets more vibrant and lush closer to Shymkent.

lm.name: A21 Kostanay-Petropavl
lm.note:

The sides of the car are unblurred most of the time.

From Kostanay to Uzunkol, the car is torn in the front left side.

Summer coverage - sunny weather.

The landscape is very vibrant and lush, you will see a lot of trees.

The landscape is quite flat.

lm.name: A22 Karabutak-Kostanay
lm.note:
Undivided road with white roadlines most of the times.

The only divided part is from Rudny to Kostanay, with yellow outer lines.

Most of the times the landscape is very flat without any trees.

The northern part near Rudny and Kostanay is the only part with trees and bushes.

lm.name: A26 Sartabak-Kandyagash
lm.note:

lm.name: A27 Atyrau-Kandyagash
lm.note:

lm.name: A28 Uralsk-Inderbor
lm.note:
The road has white roadlines visible everywhere.

Unblurred sides of the car most of the times, but not everywhere

The further south you go, the less vegetation you will see.

lm.name: A33 Zhetybay-Dossor
lm.note:
One of the few roads in the south in really good conditions.

White roadlines visible everywhere.

The landscape is a flat steppe, without any vegetation.

The weather is sunny, sometimes lacks any cloudes.

lm.name: A33/R114 Zhanaozen-Aktau
lm.note:
The only divided highway in the south, with white roadlines.

The landscape is very wet, steppe, with just a few shrubs visible along the road.

Sometimes somewhat sandy hills can be seen.

lm.name: A36 Astana-Karaganda
lm.note:
Divided highway with yellow outer lines.

The weather is overcast most of the times.

The landscape is very flat with small amount of vegetation.

Summer coverage, but feels more like autumn.

lm.name: E38 Aktobe-Karabutak
lm.note:
The road is not in the best conditions.

White roadlines, but mostly only the inner lines are visible.

The sides of the car are unblurred.

The weather is sunny.

The landscape is flat with small amount of vegetation.

lm.name: E38 Kyzylorda-Sartabak
lm.note:
The road is in quite good conditions, with white roadlines visible most of the times.

In the north the weather is overcast, in the south is sunny, mostly without any cloudes.

In the north, the landscape is very flat and dry, the vegetation consists only of small clusters along the road.

In the south near Kyzylorda, the landscape is still very flat, but the vegetation is very lush, with a lot of green shrubs. However, trees are still quite rare in this region.

lm.name: E38 Shymkent-Kyzylorda
lm.note:
Divided highway in good conditions, with white roadlines.

The weather is sunny almost everytime.

The landscape si very flat and dry most of the times.

The only divided part in near Aktobe.

lm.name: M36 Karaganda-Almaty
lm.note: The section of the M36 going from Karaganda to Almaty can often be recognised by the road being under construction, with a second lane being built. Yellow lines are common. As for the landscape, it’s a wintery dry steppe, which looks noticeably orange-brown.

lm.name: M38 Pavlodar-Semey
lm.note:
The road is in good condition, with white roadlines visible almost everytime.

The coverage was captured in autumn, so eveything looks noticeably yellow-orange-brown.

The weather is sunny, everything is quite dry.

Near Semey, the road is divided and runs through pine forest.

The landscape is very flat.

lm.name: P103 Inderbor-Atyrau
lm.note:
The road lacks roadlines, but the pavement is in quite good conditions.

Summer coverage, the weather is sunny.

The landscape is flat and rather dry, with almost no vegetation.

Only shrubs and cluster are common, the trees are very rare (but you can see them in the south near Atyrau).

lm.name: P4/A17 Astana-Pavlodar
lm.note:
Divided highway with yellow outer lines (only near Pavlodar the outer lines are white).

The coverage goes both directions (both in autumn), so the images can vary depending on the direction.

In general, the weather is overcast, only near Pavlodar it is sunny.

The landscape is flat, trees are not so common, you will see mostly just shrubs.

lm.name: A Type Car
lm.note:
Car meta is, for better or worse, a powerful way to narrow down your guesses in Kazakhstan. In this map, you will first learn to distinguish the basic types of car. You can get used to doing a quick check on every round: Season, car, driving direction. Once you are familiar with these identifications, the second map in the series will go into detail on how to best use that info.

A Type has a slender black rubber antenna. You can tell that a wire spirals around it under the rubber one or two times. It is also called the "screw antenna". In the left forward corner of the truck bed, there is a metal bracket mounted directly to the side of the truck. It can hold a wire, but the wire doesn't change the type of car.

lm.name: Aktau vibes
lm.note: Light yellow brick. Sand. The sea to the West and a bit of elevation. Gold-rimmed white street signs with Cyrillic and Latin text. Summer coverage, bright skies. Aktau!

lm.name: Almaty vibes
lm.note: Footage in Almaty was taken in November and in the spring, so the city looks distinctly and uniquely wintery, with the occasional fresh grass coming up.

lm.name: Astana vibes
lm.note: Astana used to be called Nur-Sultan. A lot of signs still say that. It's a very large city with very large buildings, wide boulevards, and a comparatively affluent vibe, and care has been taken to make it presentable and look nice. The footage was taken in Summer, and the city is looking its best.

lm.name: Big Mountains
lm.note: The Southeast of the country is the only place with anything taller than a hill visible. The mountains reach impressive heights and the largest ridges are snowcapped.

lm.name: Birches and fields
lm.note: In the central northern part of the country, Big green fields are punctuated by copses of birches, lush and green. The roads are also often lined with rows of other trees and tall, healthy shrubs.

lm.name: C Type Car
lm.note:
Car meta is, for better or worse, a powerful way to narrow down your guesses in Kazakhstan. In this map, you will first learn to distinguish the basic types of car. You can get used to doing a quick check on every round: Season, car, driving direction. Once you are familiar with these identifications, the second map in the series will go into detail on how to best use that info.

C Type has an antenna with a stubby look, with many tiny ridges. It is also called the "rattlesnake antenna". This car can have a bracket, a wire in the truck bed, or a support bar across the back edge of the cabin. All of these combinations count as C Type.

lm.name: D Type Car
lm.note:
Car meta is, for better or worse, a powerful way to narrow down your guesses in Kazakhstan. In this map, you will first learn to distinguish the basic types of car. You can get used to doing a quick check on every round: Season, car type, wire, driving direction. Once you are familiar with these identifications, the second map in the series will go into detail on how to best use that info.

D Type actually has the same antenna type as C Type, but it is folded backward to point directly at the camera. This car can have a bracket, a wire in the truck bed, or a support bar across the back edge of the cabin. All of these combinations count as D Type.

lm.name: Desert and Shrubs
lm.note: Sandy soil, very arid landscapes and small, dry-looking bushes dominate the Southwest of the country.

lm.name: Fall
lm.note:
Google started covering Kazakhstan in August 22 in the capital, Astana, and basically went around the country clockwise over the next year. The changing seasons over that year are a great clue for where in the country you are.

During the fall, Google covered the Northeast. It can be tricky to tell late summer and early fall apart, but generally, things start looking just a little more wilted and less lush and, for lack of a better word, juicy, Once fall is in full swing, there is seldom any doubt about the season: lots of deciduous trees show off their colors, and things start to look more and more orange.

lm.name: Fall hills
lm.note: In the East Kazakhstan Region, north of Oskemen, footage was taken of sometimes quite substantial hills during fall. If you see red leaves and hills, this is where you should guess.

lm.name: Golden hills
lm.note: In the central southern part of the country, by the Usbek border near Shymkent, you will find rolling hills with golden grass. Further east, you will start to see big mountains in the distance and the hills will be more green. Further south, the landscape becomes drier, flatter again, and then more agricultural.

lm.name: Green hills
lm.note: Between Shymkent and Almaty, but especially northeast of Bishkek, you will find hills with green grass on them, sometimes with bigger mountains visible in the distance. The hills range from the wide and rolling to an almost Scottish-looking landscape.

lm.name: Green plains
lm.note: All over the Northwest, vast, flat open plains with green grass can be found. Occasional groups of trees and bushes can dot the landscape or line the road for a little stretch, especially around civilization. Around Aktobe, in the West, the landscape can become a tiny bit less flat.

lm.name: No Antenna/Blurred Car
lm.note:
Car meta is, for better or worse, a powerful way to narrow down your guesses in Kazakhstan. In this map, you will first learn to distinguish the basic types of car. You can get used to doing a quick check on every round: Season, car, driving direction. Once you are familiar with these identifications, the second map in the series will go into detail on how to best use that info.

Throughout the whole country, and independently of the car type, the antenna can have been removed using image processing, or the car been blurred. In some cases, you will still be able to tell which antenna type it is by the reflection in the car's roof or other features of the car (for instance, if you see a support bar or no bracket, it cannot be Type A or B), but sometimes not. "No antenna" is not its own type of car, just obscured information. "Blurred car" likewise is not its own category, but it can be useful for identifying a small number of places that get it very consistently for longer stretches.

lm.name: Oskemen vibes
lm.note: Oskemen was covered in October, so the leaves are perhaps a little further along in their color change than in the otherwise similar-looking Pavlodar and Semey. Another way to tell the three apart are the buses: Oskemen uses a variety of buses in different colors, while the ones in Pavlodar are all green and those in Semey are all green with a white bottom. In any event, fall coverage in a big city should only be in Pavlodar, Semey or Oskemen.

lm.name: Pavlodar vibes
lm.note: Pavlodar was covered in September, so the leaves are in the process of turning orange, but it doesn't feel too cold yet. It's kind of pleasant and sunny, which can be an indicator to tell it apart from the otherwise similar-looking Semey. In any event, fall coverage in a big city should only be in Pavlodar, Semey or Oskemen.

lm.name: Ridder vibes
lm.note: The twin towns of Ridder and Leninogorsk are situated in a flat valley, surrounded by substantial mountains which are visible from almost everywhere. There are a lot of wooden houses on the outskirts, and the area looks fairly dreary. The inner city does have bigger apartment blocks. The footage was taken in fall, with orange leaves.

lm.name: Semey vibes
lm.note: Semey was covered in September, with leaves just starting to turn orange. You will find a lot of brick facades with contrasty mortar, and many houses feature blue elements. Dark wooden houses are also common. The city uses a unique livery on their buses, green with a white bottom. The footage looks perhaps a little less sunny than the otherwise similar Pavlodar. In any event, fall coverage in a big city should only be in Pavlodar, Semey or Oskemen.

lm.name: Shymkent vibes
lm.note: Freshly sprouted lush bright green leaves and grass characterize the April footage in Shymkent. There is a certain grayness to the atmosphere. (Frustratingly, some summer coverage exists in the city, too.) The city center features wide boulevards with trees planted between lanes. The architecture of the suburbs has mostly low wide slanted roofs, while garages frequently have rounded roofs. Colorful houses are relatively common, some of the neighbourhoods are even color-coordinated. Shymkent is one of just three cities that have prominent yellow electricity boxes.

lm.name: Snow coverage
lm.note: There will be snow on the ground, sometimes a fully white field and sometimes just a few almost-molten remains, around, in, and east of Almaty, in the Southeast.

lm.name: Summer
lm.note:
Google started covering Kazakhstan in August 22 in the capital, Astana, and basically went around the country clockwise over the next year. The changing seasons over that year are a great clue for where in the country you are.

The whole western half was covered in June and July, bigger plants (where available) are in full deep green foliage and there's a palpable sense of heat in many areas. In the more deserty areas, things look deserty, but even there you get green tufts of grass sometimes. The grass turns yellow a little earlier than the trees, so it can be tricky to discern it from fall coverage sometimes, especially in August footage in the central and northern part of Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Support bar
lm.note:
Car meta is, for better or worse, a powerful way to narrow down your guesses in Kazakhstan. In this map, you will first learn to distinguish the basic types of car. You can get used to doing a quick check on every round: Season, car, driving direction. Once you are familiar with these identifications, the second map in the series will go into detail on how to best use that info.

The back edge of the cabin roof can sport an additional white bar sometimes. This will only ever be on C or D type car, A and B do not have the bar.

lm.name: Wavy steppe
lm.note: In a large area around Karaganda, the landscape is mostly an empty steppe with very slight hills, if you can even call most of them that. It's just not completely flat, but sort of wavy. You get bits of vegetation other than grass in some parts, but not a whole lot. Most of this area was covered in late summer and early fall, so the grass is changing color. The big exception is the road south out of Karaganda, which was covered in November and is noticeably more wintery.

lm.name: Winter & Spring
lm.note:
Google started covering Kazakhstan in August 22 in the capital, Astana, and basically went around the country clockwise over the next year. The changing seasons over that year are a great clue for where in the country you are.

The winter coverage starts in November, leaving Karaganda south toward Almaty. The grass is brown and dead-looking, the trees are barren. Coverage then continues in early spring (March and eventually April), exploring the Southeast of the country and ending up back where the journey started, in Turkistan. Trees will sometimes still be barren, or producing the first buds and even bright green leaves. The grass is springing up lush and green in parts already. Much of this season is still covered in snow.

lm.name: Wire
lm.note:
Car meta is, for better or worse, a powerful way to narrow down your guesses in Kazakhstan. In this map, you will first learn to distinguish the basic types of car. You can get used to doing a quick check on every round: Season, car, driving direction. Once you are familiar with these identifications, the second map in the series will go into detail on how to best use that info.

In the left forward corner of the truck bed, sometimes there will be a thick black wire or cable. It can be a single thread, or a spool.

lm.name: "Zigzag"
lm.note:
On the P24 between Oskemen and Semey, as well as in both cities, you can spot this “zigzag” shaped smudge on the left side of the car.

NOTE: The smudge is highlighted in the image, and will not appear pink on street view.

lm.name: 3 Dots (1)
lm.note: This combination of 3 dots; 2 of which are close together near the back of the roof, and a third one above to the left, can be found in the coverage north of Zhezqazghan, but not in the city itself.

lm.name: 3 Dots (2)
lm.note: Around Kyzylorda, there is another combination of 3 dots; one on the bottom right, and 2 dots side by side, closer to the middle.

lm.name: A1 Highway
lm.note:
The section of the A1 going from Astana to Shchuchinsk is a 6-lane divided highway. The landscape around is generally quite green, with trees and grassy plains or hills.

Driving direction: Both ways

lm.name: A17 Highway
lm.note:
The A17 going to Ulytau Region can be recognised by the bad pavement quality, where the edges of the road are almost crumbling away, along with the single white middle road line, which can be dashed or solid. The landscape itself is a grassy steppe, with some fall coloured trees occasionally lining the roads.

West of Atasu, the sun is distinctly low on the horizon.

NOTE: A small section east of Atasu has pristine new pavement, which has a slight red tint to it.

lm.name: A26 Highway
lm.note:
The A26 goes from Kandyagash to the intersection of M32/E38.

It has very bad road quality throughout, ranging from poor grainy pavement, to completely unpaved. Apart from the northernmost section, the weather is either cloudy or overcast.

The landscape consists mostly of flat, semi-arid grassy plains.

lm.name: A3/P130 Highway
lm.note:
The roads from Kyzylagash to Druzhba feature a unique hilly landscape, which looks hazy and dead. On most sections, you will see small mountains either south or east of the road.

Driving direction: East from Kyzylagash.

lm.name: Akmola Pole Paint
lm.note: Akmola region has a very thin layer of red, then white, and a thin layer of black on the bottom.

lm.name: Aktobe Bus
lm.note: Aktobe uses orange and black buses.

lm.name: Aktobe Street Sign
lm.note: Aktobe has compact signs where half of the space is taken by the QR code.

lm.name: Almaty Bus
lm.note: Almaty uses fully green buses, with white patterns and the city name on the sides. Taraz can use similar buses, but they will have “Taraz” written on the sides instead.

lm.name: Altyn Emel National Park
lm.note: The Altyn Emel National Park is a barren grassland with snowy mountains in all directions. Some parts are very snowy. And in the eastern section, there is a small curvy mountain pass.

lm.name: Astana Bus
lm.note: Astana commonly uses these white, black, and green electric buses.

lm.name: Astana Street Sign
lm.note: Astana consistently uses this fairly generic design.

lm.name: Atyrau Bus Stop
lm.note: Atyrau has a modern design, with white and lime/neon green walls. The bus stop name is prominently written on top.

lm.name: Atyrau Pole Paint
lm.note:
Atyrau Region uses blue, white, and black paint.

This pole paint can only be found in the cities of Inderbor, Dossor and Atyrau. (All in Atyrau region)

lm.name: Atyrau Traffic Light Post
lm.note:
A couple of times you will see this Traffic Light Posts. These Posts are exclusive to the city of Atyrau.

NOTE: This meta works only 99% of cases.

lm.name: Baltic Pine Forests
lm.note:
Coverage in dense baltic pine forests can be found north of Shchuchinsk, which is north of Astana.

NOTE: Baltic pines can be found in other parts of the country.

lm.name: Black and White Curbs
lm.note: The city of Kostanay has a lot of these Black and White curbs. In almost every location, you will see these curbs.

lm.name: Blue Roof
lm.note:
In the city of Aktobe there are a lot of houses with blue roofs.

NOTE: Please don't use this meta if you see only one blue roof. Almost every other city in Kazakhstan has also houses with blue roofs.

lm.name: Coating of Dirt
lm.note: Between Kokshetau and Atbasar, the car has a thin coating of dirt and dust, which is most visible near the back of the roof.

lm.name: Desert Landscape
lm.note: Sandy and shrubby desert-like landscapes are common in southwestern Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Dirty Car
lm.note:
In the highlighted coverage east of Almaty, the back of the roof is very dirty.

NOTE: Similar dirty cars can be found in some nearby cities.

lm.name: E38 Highway
lm.note:
The divided section of the E38 goes southeast to northwest from Shymkent to Kyzylorda. The road is made of asphalt, and it has all white road lines. The landscape varies quite a lot; in the south, it is very green and in the north, it gets dry, sandy, and shrubby.

Driving direction: Both ways

lm.name: Ekibastuz Pole Paint
lm.note: Ekibastuz has a thin layer of blue, and white

lm.name: Faint Dot
lm.note:
South of Beyneu, there is a faint dot on the middle-right of the roof.

NOTE: This dot along with other smudges can be found in some nearby cities.

lm.name: Green Plains
lm.note: Vast grassy green plains are found in northwestern Kazakhstan. They are especially common in Akmola and Kostanay regions.

lm.name: Hazy Forest Fire Coverage
lm.note: Parts of Oskemen have hazy forest fire coverage.

lm.name: Hilly + Dry
lm.note: The landscape in southern Kazakhstan near Uzbekistan is hilly and quite dry and shrubby, with a lot of orange looking grass. The landscape consists of dry but grassy rolling hills or dead flat agricultural land near Zhetisay.

lm.name: Hilly + Forested
lm.note: The East Kazakhstan Region is hilly and forested. It was covered in october, so you will see fall colours on the vegetation. The town of Ridder itself is flat, but surrounded by hazy mountains.

lm.name: Karaganda Bus
lm.note: Karaganda uses turquoise buses, just like their bus stops.

lm.name: Karaganda Bus Stop
lm.note: Karaganda uses old looking turquoise bus stops, which have a curved roof.

lm.name: Kentau Pole Paint
lm.note: Kentau poles have thin layers of blue, yellow, and red, then blue and black below them.

lm.name: Kokshetau Pole Paint
lm.note: Kokshetau uses a few designs, but they all have light blue on the bottom, and sometimes, a thin strip, or two, of yellow on top.

lm.name: Kostanay Bus Stop
lm.note: Kostanay uses simple brown bus stops, that have a blue and yellow crest on one of the glass panes.

lm.name: Kostanay Pole Paint
lm.note: Kostanay uses a thin layer of turqoise, and yellow.

lm.name: Kulsary Lamp
lm.note: Lamps in Kulsary have a sizable blue photocell on the top.

lm.name: Kyrgyz KM Marker
lm.note: These red and white KM markers that look like Kyrgyz ones, are only found near Zhetisay.

lm.name: Kyzylorda Lamp Post Paint
lm.note: Kyzylorda lamp posts are white, and have turquoise on the bottom.

lm.name: Kyzylorda Pole Paint
lm.note: Kyzylorda poles have a thin layer of yellow and red, then white.

lm.name: Line of Dirt
lm.note: East of Aktobe, there is a vertical line of dirt on the right side of the roof.

lm.name: Lush Birch Forest
lm.note:
These lush birch forests next to green fields are common in northern Kazakhstan.

NOTE: This landscape often appears very similar to that found in and around Omsk Oblast in Russia.

lm.name: M36 Highway (1)
lm.note:
Between Karaganda and Astana, the M36 is now a divided highway, with yellow outer lines. The landscape consists of a grassy, sometimes hilly, steppe with an occasional row of trees along the road. Note that the general southeast to northwest road angle is important.

Driving direction: Both ways

lm.name: M36 Highway (2)
lm.note:
The section of the M36 going from Karaganda to Almaty can often be recognised by the road being under construction, with a second lane being built. Yellow lines are common. As for the landscape, it’s a wintery dry steppe, which looks noticeably orange-brown.

Driving direction: South from Karaganda.

lm.name: May Coverage
lm.note: The only May coverage in Kazakhstan is found in the Almaty exclave of Alataou, which is east of Almaty proper. All of the coverage is sunny and the mountains are visible to the south.

lm.name: P4/A17 Highway
lm.note:
The P4/A17 from Astana to Pavlodar is a divided road, generally going east to west, through a hilly steppe landscape similar to the M36, but is generally less vegetated. Most of the road has outer yellow lines.

Driving direction: Both ways

lm.name: Pavlodar Pole Marking
lm.note: This exclusive pole marking can only be found in Pavlodar.

lm.name: Petropavl Bus Stop
lm.note: Petropavl also has brown bus stops, with glass panes on all 3 sides not facing the road. The roof is angled slightly upwards.

lm.name: Petropavl Pole Paint
lm.note: Petropavl has a thin layer of white, and light grey.

lm.name: Petropavl Street Sign
lm.note: Petropavl uses white signs, with a blue semicircle below the street names.

lm.name: Pine Trees
lm.note: Around Semey, you can find small clusters or entire forests consisting mostly of pine trees and some deciduous trees, which will have fall colours.

lm.name: R260 road
lm.note:
The R260 road is mostly paved, but not in the best condition; many cracks can be seen, and it mostly lacks road lines. The weather is overcast and the landscape is a slightly hilly steppe, consisting of somewhat yellow grass and reddish soil, which is very evident when the road is unpaved.

The R217 is very similar, but the road is in better condition and mostly has very faded dashed white middle road lines, which are often quite difficult to see. The further east you go, the more sparse the cloud cover gets.

Driving directions: South from Atbasar

lm.name: Road of Zhezgazghan
lm.note:
The road north of Zhezqazghan has no road lines. The landscape is very dry, desolate, with very limited vegetation and slightly hilly. The soil can look very red or orange at times.

The weather is sunny, with a lot of cumulus clouds.

Driving directions: North from Nikolskiy

lm.name: Rolling grassy hills
lm.note: Grassy green rolling hills can be found in southern Kazakhstan. They are especially common just north of Bishkek

lm.name: Rudny Pole Paint
lm.note: Rudny has red, yellow, red on the top, with white below it.

lm.name: Semey Bus
lm.note: Semey has these light green and white buses.

lm.name: Shchuchinsk Pole Paint
lm.note: Shchuchinsk has a thin layer of red, and yellow.

lm.name: Shymkent Pole Paint
lm.note: Shymkent poles have a thin layer of yellow and red, then green.

lm.name: Small Ridge of Hills
lm.note: A small ridge of hills is visible to the north in a lot of Taldykorgan coverage.

lm.name: Small Smudge
lm.note: Between Petropavl and Kokshetau, there is a small smudge slightly to the left on the bottom of the roof.

lm.name: Snow Coverage
lm.note: Snow coverage can be found in southeastern Kazakhstan, especially east of Almaty.

lm.name: Snow Coverage in Mountains
lm.note: In southern Almaty City, there is snow coverage in the mountains.

lm.name: Speckled Roof
lm.note: On the borderroad from Kazakhstan to Uzbekistan, the google truck has a distinct speckled roof.

lm.name: Tall Mountains
lm.note: Tall mountains, which are often snow-capped, can be seen in southeastern Kazakhstan.

lm.name: Taraz Pole Paint
lm.note: Taraz has red, yellow, and black.

lm.name: Turkistan Lamp
lm.note: Turkistan consistently uses these thin grey lamps with two small light sources near the end.

lm.name: Unpaved Sandy Desert Road
lm.note: Near the Turkmenistan border in southwest Kazakhstan, you will find this unpaved sandy desert road. The landscape is almost blindingly bright from the sand.

lm.name: Uralsk Lamp
lm.note: Some lamps in Uralsk have this very unique design, with 3 separate lamps in an ascending pattern.

lm.name: Visible Wire
lm.note: A visible wire in the back of the Street View car can be found in all of western Kazakhstan.

lm.name: West Kazakhstan Pole Paint
lm.note: West Kazakhstan Region uses red, white, and black paint.

lm.name: Yellow Boxes
lm.note:
Yellow boxes connected to the gas pipes are common outside houses in Shymkent, Turkistan, and Taldykorgan.

NOTE: In Shymkent the boxes are almost completely silver. In Turkistan, the boxes have a faded yellow color. And in Taldykorgan, the boxes are completely yellow (They look very new).

lm.name: Zhetisay Street Sign
lm.note: Zhetisay also uses a fairly generic design, but it is not found in Turkistan or Shymkent.

lm.name: Zhezqazghan Bus
lm.note: Zhezqazghan has orange and white buses, with “Men ♥ Jezz/Zhez” written on the sides.

top.html:
Kazakhstan uses both Cyrillic and Latin alphabets.

Though sometimes, Russian is used monolingually.

  • The following letters are found in the Kazakh but not Russian alphabet: Ә (Ä), Ғ (Ǵ), Қ (Q), Ң (Ń), Ө (Ö), Ұ (W), Ү (Ü), Һ (H), І (I).
  • Kazakh is related to Turkish, so the Latin text can appear similar.

top.html:
Kazakhstan is a big and diverse country, which features a plethora of distinct landscapes like deserts, grassy steppes, mountain passes, and birch forests.

Most strikingly, most of the rural coverage in Kazakhstan is in a very empty, open and mostly flat landscape.
top.raw: Kazakhstan is a big and diverse country, which features a plethora of distinct landscapes like [deserts](https://goo.gl/maps/DWJvw2JjfZTTF2ER9), [grassy steppes](https://goo.gl/maps/FtuwHnxx1cACr5HU9), [mountain passes](https://goo.gl/maps/dnJR7qdEBDQLUkUC9), and [birch forests](https://goo.gl/maps/NTfW9tkDsF2mVbqT8). Most strikingly, most of the rural coverage in Kazakhstan is in a very empty, open and mostly flat landscape.

top.html: A lot of Kazakh infrastructure, from pedestrian signs, poles, houses, to bollards, is very similar to what you see in Russia.
top.raw: A lot of Kazakh infrastructure, from pedestrian signs, poles, houses, to bollards, is very similar to what you see in Russia.

top.html: Like Russia, Kazakhstan uses yellow and white stripes on their pedestrian crossings. However, unlike Russia the stripes often have white dashes on either side. Sometimes, you can find the dashes without the stripes.
top.raw: Like Russia, Kazakhstan uses **yellow and white stripes** on their pedestrian crossings. However, unlike Russia the stripes often have white dashes on either side. Sometimes, you can find the [dashes](https://goo.gl/maps/sXKtyw86YGYSEKLY9) without the stripes.

top.html:
Street Signs in Kazakhstan are often attached to buildings and are blue in colour, with white intricate patterns on the top and bottom. They are usually bilingual or trilingual and can also contain a QR code.

NOTE: They are often inconsistent, with many designs being found in a single city.
top.raw: Street Signs in Kazakhstan are often attached to buildings and are **blue **in colour, with white intricate patterns on the top and bottom. They are usually **bilingual or trilingual** and can also contain a **QR code**. NOTE: They are often inconsistent, with many designs being found in a single city.

top.html: Kazakhstan uses a variety of post-Soviet style bollards, as well as ones that resemble Turkish bollards. Notably, the bollards seemingly consisting of two thin bollards attached at a 90° angle are unique to Kazakhstan.
top.raw: Kazakhstan uses a variety of post-Soviet style bollards, as well as ones that resemble Turkish bollards. Notably, the bollards seemingly consisting of two thin bollards attached at a **90° angle** are unique to Kazakhstan.

top.html:
The bottom of tree trunks are very often painted white.

NOTE: This is common in several eastern European countries, as well as in parts of Russia.
